key_facts: **Solar lentigines** ('liver spots', 'age spots') are flat, well-defined brown macules on sun-exposed skin.
Face, backs of hands, forearms and shoulders in middle-aged and older adults; a marker of sun damage.
Dermoscopy: fine reticular pattern, 'moth-eaten' edges, fingerprint pattern.
Differentiate from **lentigo maligna** (irregular, enlarging, multiple colours on the face) and pigmented AK or SK.
Benign: sun protection; cryotherapy or laser are cosmetic options.

sections.title: Overview
blocks: **Solar lentigines** (“age spots”, “liver spots”) are benign flat tan-to-dark-brown macules on chronically sun-exposed skin. They mark cumulative UV damage and skin-cancer risk but are not themselves premalignant.

sub: Over 90% of fair-skinned people over 60; increase with age and sun exposure.

sections.title: Aetiology: causes and risk factors
blocks: UV-driven localised melanocyte hyperactivity. Risk rises with fair skin, outdoor work, sunburn history, sunbeds and age.

ul: Chronic UV exposure; PUVA and sunbeds produce similar lentigines.
**"They're harmless so never need checking"**: a changing, irregular facial lentigo may be lentigo maligna.

sections.title: Pathophysiology and pathology
blocks: UV causes a **local increase in melanocytes** and pigment along the basal layer.

mech.t: Repeated UV exposure stimulates basal melanocytes.
Melanocyte numbers increase modestly along the basal layer (no nests).
Rete ridges lengthen and are heavily pigmented, creating a flat brown patch.

histo: Elongated, club-shaped, pigmented rete ridges with a slight increase in single basal melanocytes; no atypia.

ul: Uniform light-to-dark brown macules with a regular border; face, dorsal hands, forearms, shoulders.
May coexist with AK field change and photoageing.

sub: Asymmetric pigmentation, multiple colours, grey dots, enlargement: refer via the suspected cancer pathway.

sections.title: Diagnosis and investigations
blocks: Clinical ± dermoscopy (fingerprint/moth-eaten border patterns). Biopsy or refer asymmetric, irregular, enlarging, ugly-duckling or grey-regression lesions — especially on the face.

ddx.name: Melasma
ddx.f: Symmetrical patches; hormones; worsened by heat/IPL — see [melasma](condition:melasma-facial-melanosis)

ddx.name: Lentigo maligna
ddx.f: Irregular colours, slow enlargement on older face → NG12 referral

ul: Daily broad-spectrum SPF 30–50 (± tinted); hats/gloves for driving and gardening — without this, treated lesions return.
Examine the whole photodamaged field for AK/BCC/SCC/lentigo maligna.
Modest topicals: retinoids, azelaic acid; short specialist hydroquinone courses only (ochronosis risk).
Procedural (usually private): light cryotherapy (hypopigmentation risk, especially in darker skin), pigment laser for discrete spots, IPL for diffuse pigment+redness — only after diagnosis is secure.
Melasma is a poor IPL indication and can worsen.

refer.t: Any lesion suspicious for lentigo maligna or melanoma → urgent suspected-cancer pathway.
Do not treat undiagnosed pigment with cryotherapy, IPL or laser.

sections.title: Red flags and when to refer

ul: Any lesion suspicious for lentigo maligna or melanoma → urgent suspected-cancer pathway.
Do not treat undiagnosed pigment with cryotherapy, IPL or laser.
Cosmetic concern; may evolve into a flat seborrhoeic keratosis (reticulated SK).
Persist and increase; fade slightly with strict sun protection.

pearls: Solar lentigines are a UV dosimeter — use the visit for skin-cancer education.
Hand spots are a classic patient question; same rules as the face.

Flat brown marks that become raised and warty are usually [seborrhoeic keratoses](condition:seborrhoeic-keratosis); a lentigo that darkens or spreads unevenly on the face may be [lentigo maligna](condition:melanoma).

quiz.q: When should you think of Solar lentigines?
quiz.a: Flat, evenly brown macules on the face or backs of the hands of an older outdoor worker that do not fade in winter.
Chronic UV increases local melanocyte number and activity along elongated rete ridges.

quiz.q: What is the backbone of care?
quiz.a: Photoprotection forever; topical retinoids/azelaic acid for modest fading; cryotherapy/IPL/laser only after cancer exclusion — usually private.
Irregular, multicoloured, enlarging facial pigment → lentigo maligna — urgent suspected-cancer referral. Never laser an undiagnosed pigmented lesion.

quiz.q: Name a red flag that needs escalation.
quiz.a: Any lesion suspicious for lentigo maligna or melanoma → urgent suspected-cancer pathway.
